what_its_for: Niraparib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer, or peritoneal cancer (cancer in the lining of the belly). It works by blocking a protein that helps cancer cells repair themselves, which slows or stops cancer growth. Your doctor may prescribe it to help keep your cancer from coming back after chemotherapy, or as a first treatment for advanced cancer.
how_to_take: Take niraparib by mouth (swallow the capsule whole) once a day, with or without food. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. If nausea bothers you, try taking it at bedtime. Do not open, crush, or chew the capsules.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your dose based on your weight and blood platelet levels. The usual starting dose is either 200 mg or 300 mg once daily. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribed. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it is still the same day, take it as soon as you remember. If you vomit after taking a dose, do NOT take an extra dose — just wait and take your next scheduled dose as usual. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose entirely. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store niraparib at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed and away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming pregnant while taking niraparib — it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for 1 month after stopping. Avoid activities that require sharp alertness (like driving) if you feel dizzy or confused. Let your doctor know about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some may interact with niraparib.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: unusual bruising or bleeding, extreme tiredness or weakness, shortness of breath, pale skin, rapid heart rate, signs of low blood counts (fever, chills, infections), severe headache or confusion, high blood pressure, chest pain, sudden numbness or vision changes, or any new or worsening symptoms. These could be signs of serious side effects that need prompt attention. Go to the emergency room or call 911 if you have a medical emergency.
when_it_works: Niraparib starts working in your body right away, but you may not feel a difference immediately since it works to control cancer at the cellular level. It is important to keep taking it every day as prescribed, even if you feel well. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests, especially during the first year of treatment, to check that the medicine is working and that your blood counts are safe.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use niraparib if you are pregnant — it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for 6 months after stopping. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine or for 1 month after your last dose. Older adults (age 75 and older): This medicine can be used in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you more closely for side effects. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver issues, as your dose may need to be adjusted. This medicine is not approved for use in children.
